rows.verified: Rubber processing can expose workers to hazardous rubber dust and fume that must be controlled under COSHH.
Health studies have identified increased cancer risk in rubber-processing stages that produce dust and fume.
Rubber production uses powerful machinery capable of causing fatal or serious injuries.
Unplanned interventions to adjust equipment or clear blockages have increased incident potential.
Safeguarding should keep operators separated from dangerous moving parts until equipment is in a safe condition.
Suitable safeguards may include perimeter fencing with interlocked access or close guarding with locking and trip devices.
Safe electrical isolation is the preferred reliable control against unexpected start-up during dangerous interventions.
Machine isolators should be locked off during maintenance unless an equally reliable engineered safety system is justified.
Rubber risk depends on compound chemistry, dust and fume generation, machine energy, intervention type, isolation reliability and maintenance condition.
Rubber evidence is compound-, process-, machine-, intervention- and worker-specific and is not an exact parcel-level cancer or injury probability.
Plastics are commonly processed as pellets, granules or powders containing additives such as fillers, pigments, fire retardants and stabilisers.
Fume composition varies with the plastic and additives, but plastics fume can severely irritate eyes, nose and lungs and may cause occupational asthma.
Local exhaust ventilation can greatly reduce health risks from plastics dust and fume.
Major plastics-industry safety areas include machinery, slips and trips, work at height and fire.
Many cellular plastics ignite readily, can spread fire quickly and may produce large volumes of thick toxic smoke.
Some plastics can continue smouldering after the main fire is extinguished.
HSE guidance covers safeguarding at injection moulding, blow moulding, thermoforming and extruder machinery.
Plastics employers should assess work activities, maintain a health-and-safety policy and keep machinery and controls safe.
Plastics risk depends on polymer and additive chemistry, processing temperature, fume generation, machine design, ignition sources, storage and ventilation.
Plastics evidence is polymer-, process-, machine-, fire-scenario- and exposure-specific and is not an exact parcel-level incident probability.
